agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 is the superscription; the KJV counts it as verse 0 (its '85:1' is Hebrew verse 2). Dramatic text renders it as a spoken heading rather than leaving it out.

I did not try to settle Ibn Ezra's and Meiri's claim that the glory 'was not in the Second Temple'; this is a rabbinic tradition (Meiri cites a Talmudic list of five things missing) and I pass it on only as attributed.

agent_notes: The last line is genuinely ambiguous: 'and he/it will set (the way) for the way of his footsteps'. The subject of 'sets' may be YHWH, or Righteousness (Malbim, Rashi's reading with YHWH setting Righteousness in his paths), and the object is left implicit. KJV supplies 'us', which is not in the Hebrew (Webster brackets it). I kept the Hebrew's open syntax in the literal layer and, in the dramatic layer, chose the reading where Righteousness makes a road for his footsteps (as YLT, BBE).
Ibn Ezra's suggestion that 'tzedek' stands for 'a man of righteousness' (with 'ish' omitted) is quoted from the packet; I did not adopt it.

agent_notes: Written שבות (Ketiv, 'restoration/captivity'), read שבית (Qere). The packet table shows the Qere; I glossed the reading. Radak and Meiri both say the two are one in sense. 'Turned the captivity' keeps the Hebrew idiom shuv shevut; the versions split between 'brought back' (KJV, ASV, Webster), 'turned to' (YLT) and BBE's 'changing the fate', which is the idiom's other sense. I kept 'turned' to preserve the shuv chain through the psalm.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses nasata as 'you forgave'; literally 'you lifted/carried'. The literal layer keeps 'lifted' and the commentary explains the metaphor. Selah is left untranslated.

heshivota is Hiphil, so strictly 'you made [it] turn back from the burning of your anger' (Radak, Meiri: the object is the anger itself). KJV 'turned thyself' follows the other reading (Ibn Ezra takes it as the intransitive sense). I chose the causative in the literal layer and noted the dispute.

agent_notes: shuvenu is Qal imperative with 1cp suffix. Rashi reads 'turn, and then bring us back'; STEPBible says 'restore us'. The verse is ambiguous between 'turn us [back to you/to the land]' and 'return to us' (YLT, BBE). I kept 'turn us' in the literal layer and put the alternatives in the commentary.

The Hebrew uses ʾaf ('nose/anger') in tamshokh ʾapkha; the root of te'enaf is the verb form of the same noun, a figura etymologica that English cannot carry. The literal layer repeats 'angry' and 'anger'. Malbim's long distinction between ʾaf and ʾanaf is his own theological reading; I did not rely on it.

Two readings of tashuv tchayenu: the KJV 'wilt thou not revive us again' takes tashuv adverbially ('again'); YLT takes it as a separate clause ('Dost Thou not turn back? Thou revivest us'). I followed the first in the dramatic layer and kept the double verbs 'turn [and] give life' in the literal layer.

agent_notes: Reviewer request applied: the note on וְיֶשְׁעֲךָ now says the segol under the yod is unusual (the usual form would be yish'akha), citing Radak and Meiri, who both remark on the pointing; Meiri's comparison with Psalm 38 is mentioned. I did not try to explain why the pointing is unusual.

Verse 8 is the hinge of the psalm: the Hebrew has an imperative (har'enu) and then an imperfect (titten). English versions split: KJV and ASV make both a request ('grant us'), YLT makes the second a statement ('Thou dost give'). I kept the imperfect as a plea, as the paired request in the clause suggests, and say so in the commentary.
